description:
JDollar, a solo builder who ships products your grandma can use. 

For NASA Space Apps 2026 I built Flown, a browser game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge: you design a spacecraft to a real mission brief, pin the risks before launch, then fly into failures that really happened, drawn from NASA's own records. 
Skills: game design, TypeScript, React, three.js and space mission history.
summary:
Flown is a free browser game where you design a space mission and every way it can fail is a failure that really happened, drawn from NASA's own records. 

You build to a real mission brief, inside about the real budget, choosing power, antenna, engine, instruments, rocket, orbit and how much testing you can afford. 

Before launch you get four pins for the risks you see, and you pay to fix the ones you believe in. 
Then you fly, and real failures strike when your choices invite them: skip the end to end interface check and you can arrive far too low, like Mars Climate Orbiter; fly an unfolding dish without a flight like test and it can jam, like Galileo. 

In a real crisis you make the call, then see what the real team chose. 
Every failure opens its real case file with sources, and you can refly the same flight to prove your fix holds. 

It matters because NASA's Inspector General found only 57% of NASA flight project managers used NASA's own lessons database, and students learn spacecraft one part at a time. 

Flown makes those lessons something you learn by losing, before launch day.
details:
Flown answers the Space Mission Design Game challenge with one loop: design, review, fly, learn, fly again.

1. Build to a real brief. Six missions modeled on real ones (orbit Jupiter, map Mars from orbit, hunt planets, fly past Pluto, orbit Mercury, land on Mars), three difficulty levels.

Seven part groups, instruments, four engineering process choices (interface checks, deployment tests, fault simulation, fuel margin), launch vehicle and orbit or landing site. A live rail shows mass, cost, power, battery against shadow, data against downlink and schedule against the launch window.

2. Pin what worries you. A pre launch review with four pins. Each pin offers a fix with a real cost in money and days. Wrong pins count against you.

3. Fly into real failures. 27 real failures can strike, each triggered by design choices that match its real root cause, and each plays out on the 3D craft.
Real crises pause for your decision (Juno's helium valves, Kepler's reaction wheels, Galileo's antenna, Dawn's fuel, New Horizons' safe mode, MESSENGER's last weeks), then show what the real team chose.

4. Read the case, fix it, fly again. Every failure opens a case file: what happened, root cause, what NASA did, the lesson, sources, and your craft next to the real spacecraft. Refly the same seed to prove the fix holds. Each lesson becomes a star in your Lesson Sky; your caught before launch rate is the skill you build. A post mission analysis explains every result.

**More ways to play.**

- Play as a team: 2 to 4 friends share one spacecraft on one screen. Each person is in charge of some parts, like power or the engine. Nobody launches until everyone says GO, and when something breaks, the person in charge of that part makes the call.

- Race: friends fly the same mission one after another and compare scores.

- Challenge a friend: send a link, and your friend flies the exact same flight you did, so you can compare.

- Mission of the Day: a new mission every day, with a streak for coming back.

**How it works.** A pure TypeScript engine (budget evaluation, 27 rules mapping design choices to real lessons, a seeded deterministic flight simulator, crisis decisions, catch scoring) under a React and three.js interface.
The spacecraft is built from your parts and every failure animates on the model.

**Proof.** An answer key test proves each of the 27 failures strikes on a matching design and is prevented by its fix on the same seed (27 of 27 pass). All 38 lessons carry public sources (98 links).
Flown's mass rules are compared with NSSDCA's real spacecraft for every mission and every error is published. 56 automated tests plus browser runs of all six missions at phone and desktop width.

**Benefits and goals.** Students, teachers and space fans get system level mission design practice built on what really went wrong, with the real record one tap away.
The goal: every future engineer meets these lessons before their first launch, not after.

**Intended impact.** NASA's own Inspector General found only 57% of NASA flight project managers used NASA's lessons database.
Flown turns those lessons into something people play, remember and share, so the next generation learns them as a habit: spot the risk, pay for the fix, launch.

**How it is creative.** Most mission games invent their disasters. In Flown every failure really happened, and the main skill is not flying well but catching the problem before launch.
You pin risks, you are scored on what you caught, and you refly the exact same flight to prove your fix works.
The 3D spacecraft is built from your own parts, so you watch your dish jam the way Galileo's did. Each lesson becomes a star in your own Lesson Sky.

**Factors we considered.** Accuracy first: every failure is linked to public sources, and where we simplify for play (part values, failure odds, mass limits) the game says so on screen.
Fairness: the same seed gives the same flight, so a fix can be proven and friends can compare runs.
A gentle start: a one minute first taste (make Juno's real call), three difficulty levels and short sessions for students with no engineering background.
Access is free, in the browser, on phones and laptops, with no account and no tracking. Team play: a One craft co-op mode where each player owns a part of the spacecraft.

**How it was built.** Solo, during the hackathon, with Claude Code (an AI coding assistant) and help with gathering public sources; however every lesson keeps its source links so each fact can be checked.

**Tools.** TypeScript, React, three.js, @react-three/fiber, drei, zustand, Vite, Vitest, Playwright. Hosted on Vercel.
